beats.title: Sahelanthropus Walks the Earth
beats.description: A small-brained ape in what is now Chad may be the earliest known member of the human line, with a head balanced upright.
beats.note: Sources give about 6 to 7 million years ago; start of range used.

beats.title: Orrorin Stands on Two Legs
beats.description: An early hominin in Kenya had thigh bones built for walking upright, among the oldest signs of two-legged movement.
beats.note: 5.8 to 6.2 million years ago.

beats.title: Ardipithecus Kadabba Appears
beats.description: A woodland-dwelling early hominin in Ethiopia is the earliest known member of the Ardipithecus group.
beats.note: Oldest fossils about 5.8 million years ago.

beats.title: Ardipithecus Ramidus Appears
beats.description: A forest-dwelling hominin with grasping feet and a body adapted to both climbing and walking upright lives in Ethiopia.
beats.note: Fossils dated 4.32 to 4.51 million years ago.

beats.title: Australopithecus Anamensis Appears
beats.description: The earliest known australopith walks upright around the shores of a lake in East Africa, a likely forebear of Lucy's kind.
beats.note: Sources range 4.3 to 3.8 million years ago; 4.2 is the usual earliest.

beats.title: Footprints in Volcanic Ash
beats.description: Two or three upright walkers leave a trail of footprints across fresh ash in Tanzania, proof of habitual two-legged walking.
beats.note: Laetoli, about 3.66 million years ago.

beats.title: Kenyanthropus Appears
beats.description: A flat-faced hominin living near a lake in Kenya shares the landscape with other early species, complicating the family tree.
beats.note: Skull dated about 3.5 million years ago.

beats.title: Toolmakers Strike Stone at Lomekwi
beats.description: Early hominins in Kenya knap large stone cores and flakes, pushing tool use back before the genus Homo existed.
beats.note: Dated about 3.3 million years ago (2015 Nature study).

beats.title: Lucy, Australopithecus Afarensis
beats.description: A small, upright-walking hominin in Ethiopia lives on the grassland, later becoming the most famous early human ancestor.
beats.note: Lucy lived about 3.2 million years ago; the species itself appeared earlier.

beats.title: Australopithecus Africanus Lives
beats.description: A slender, small-brained southern African hominin with humanlike teeth walks upright and eats a varied diet.
beats.note: Sources vary: dated finds 3.0 to 2.0 million years ago, with a disputed older claim of 3.4 to 3.7; 3.0 used.

beats.title: Paranthropus Aethiopicus Appears
beats.description: The earliest of the heavy-jawed hominins evolves a huge chewing apparatus for tough plant food in East Africa.
beats.note: Range given as 2.7 to 2.3 million years ago; oldest dated remains about 2.6.

beats.title: Oldowan Stone Tools Spread
beats.description: Hominins in East Africa begin striking sharp flakes from river cobbles to cut meat and break bones for marrow.
beats.note: Gona tools dated 2.6 to 2.5 million years ago.

beats.title: Homo Habilis, the Handy Human
beats.description: A larger-brained hominin, linked with stone tools, becomes the first member of our own genus.
beats.note: Conventional start 2.4 million years ago; a 2015 jaw suggests 2.8.

beats.title: Paranthropus Boisei Appears
beats.description: A powerfully built hominin with enormous molars, nicknamed Nutcracker Man, thrives in East Africa.
beats.note: Oldest fossil (Omo jaw) about 2.3 million years ago.

beats.title: Homo Erectus Stands Tall
beats.description: A tall, long-legged human with a bigger brain and modern body proportions becomes the most widespread early human.
beats.note: Earliest fossil dated 1.95 to 2.04 million years ago; older sources say 1.8.

beats.title: Australopithecus Sediba Lives
beats.description: A mix of apelike arms and humanlike hips and teeth in a South African species raises the idea of a link to Homo.
beats.note: Malapa fossils dated 1.977 million years ago.

beats.title: Homo Ergaster Appears
beats.description: An early African form of Homo erectus, with a lean frame built for long-distance running and walking, takes shape.
beats.note: Usual start of range 1.9 million years ago; some sources say 1.8.

beats.title: Humans Leave Africa
beats.description: Small-brained early humans settle at Dmanisi in the Caucasus, the oldest known people outside the continent.
beats.note: Dmanisi about 1.8 million years ago (stone tools in China may be older, about 2.1).

beats.title: The Acheulean Handaxe Appears
beats.description: Early humans shape stone on both faces into teardrop handaxes, the first deliberately designed tool form.
beats.note: Kokiselei 4, about 1.76 million years ago (Konso about 1.7).

beats.title: Homo Antecessor Reaches Spain
beats.description: Early humans settle in southwest Europe, leaving a jaw, stone flakes and butchered bones in a cave in Atapuerca.
beats.note: Earliest remains from Sima del Elefante, about 1.2 million years ago.

beats.title: Fire Burns in Wonderwerk Cave
beats.description: Early humans burn plants and bone deep inside a South African cave, some of the oldest solid evidence of controlled fire.
beats.note: 2012 study gave about 1 million years; later dating gave a window of 1.07 to 1.79 million years.

beats.title: Fire at Gesher Benot Ya'aqov
beats.description: Early humans beside an ancient lake in the Levant repeatedly burn wood and seeds, suggesting regular hearth use.
beats.note: Dated about 790,000 years ago.

beats.title: Homo Heidelbergensis Appears
beats.description: A big-brained, strongly built human spreads across Africa and Europe and is often seen as ancestor of both Neanderthals and us.
beats.note: Start of range about 700,000 years ago, possibly 780,000.

beats.title: Neanderthals Appear
beats.description: A stocky, cold-adapted human lineage emerges in Europe and western Asia, becoming our closest extinct relatives.
beats.note: Conventional start about 400,000 years ago; estimates range 600,000 to 200,000.

beats.title: Homo Naledi Appears
beats.description: A small-brained human with curved fingers and a modern foot lives in southern Africa, alongside early Homo sapiens.
beats.note: Fossils dated 335,000 to 236,000 years ago; start of range.

beats.title: Homo Sapiens Appears
beats.description: People with the face and lightly built skull of modern humans live in North Africa, the earliest known members of our species.
beats.note: Jebel Irhoud, about 300,000 years ago.

beats.title: Early Sapiens Reach Greece
beats.description: A skull in a Greek cave appears to belong to a modern human, hinting at an early venture into Europe that left no lasting mark.
beats.note: Apidima 1, about 210,000 years ago; identification debated.

beats.title: Sapiens Settle Misliya Cave
beats.description: A jaw from a cave in the Levant shows modern humans living outside Africa far earlier than once believed.
beats.note: Dated 177,000 to 194,000 years ago.

beats.title: The Denisovans Emerge
beats.description: A mysterious branch of archaic humans lives across Asia, known mostly from teeth, a finger bone and a jaw from high-altitude caves.
beats.note: Xiahe jaw minimum age 160,000 years, matching the oldest Denisova Cave material; the lineage itself is older.

beats.title: The Last Homo Erectus
beats.description: The longest-lived human species vanishes from the island of Java after surviving far longer than our own kind has.
beats.note: Ngandong last occurrence 117,000 to 108,000 years ago (2019 study); earliest end of the window used.

beats.title: The Hobbit of Flores
beats.description: A knee-high human with a tiny brain lives on an Indonesian island, long hunting dwarf elephants and making stone tools.
beats.note: 2016 re-dating: bones 100,000 to 60,000 years old.

beats.title: Homo Luzonensis of the Philippines
beats.description: A small, tree-adapted human with curved toe bones lives on an island in Southeast Asia, later found in Callao Cave.
beats.note: Minimum ages of 50,000 and 67,000 years; earliest used.

beats.title: Humans Reach Australia
beats.description: Early sapiens cross open sea from Southeast Asia to a vast new continent, making the first ocean crossing by humans.
beats.note: Madjedbebe date of 65,000 years ago; some archaeologists suggest 55,000 to 60,000.

beats.title: Sapiens and Neanderthals Interbreed
beats.description: Modern humans and Neanderthals meet and have children together, leaving traces in the DNA of most people alive today.
beats.note: 2024 studies give about 50,500 to 43,500 years ago; start used.

beats.title: Sapiens Settle Bacho Kiro Cave
beats.description: Modern humans with ornaments and bone tools occupy a Balkan cave, the earliest well-dated people of our species in Europe.
beats.note: About 45,000 years ago.

beats.title: The Last Neanderthals
beats.description: The final Neanderthals disappear from Iberia and Europe after sharing the continent with modern humans for thousands of years.
beats.note: Disappearance placed between 45,000 and 30,000 years ago; 2014 re-dating gives about 40,000 to 39,000.

beats.title: White Sands Footprints
beats.description: Children and adults walk beside an ice-age lake in North America, leaving the oldest firm proof of people in the Americas.
beats.note: About 23,000 years ago; date still debated.
